query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloy, spatial variations in local chemical order and associated lattice strain create a broad distribution of magnetic exchange interactions that drive a sharp, first‐order magnetostructural transition with a large magnetic entropy change. However, these same chemical and structural inhomogeneities also pin magnetic domains, resulting in significant hysteresis during low‐field cooling cycles. A controlled low‐temperature annealing post‐deposition that partially homogenizes the local order and relaxes residual strains should reduce the hysteresis without drastically lowering the peak entropy change.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA, presumed to be a chemically disordered single-phase (e.g., hexagonal) solid solution with significant local compositional fluctuations and residual lattice strain.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low‐temperature annealing treatment that is sufficient to subtly enhance local chemical ordering and relax lattice strain without causing major phase transformations or grain growth.
generation.conditions: Tested under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles (e.g., fields below 1–2 T) and temperatures around the magnetostructural transition (near the alloy’s Curie temperature).
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical inhomogeneities and associated lattice strain (particularly at grain boundaries and sub-grain regions) that produce a wide distribution of magnetic exchange strengths.
generation.mechanism: The inherent non-equiatomic composition produces regions with varying magnetic exchange interactions; during field-induced cooling, these regions transition at slightly different temperatures, giving rise to a large entropy change. Simultaneously, the inhomogeneous microstructure creates energy barriers that pin domain walls, manifesting as hysteresis. Annealing partially homogenizes these regions and relaxes strains, reducing domain-pinning sites and diminishing hysteresis while keeping the magnetocaloric effect largely intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: Following the annealing intervention, the alloy will exhibit a similar magnitude of magnetic entropy change (ΔS) at the transition but with reduced hysteresis in the magnetization hysteresis loops (i.e., narrower loop width and lower coercivity), relative to the as-deposited baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited alloy shows a large but sharply peaked magnetic entropy change accompanied by significant hysteresis during low-field magnetic cooling cycles.
generation.boundary: This behavior is anticipated within processing conditions that retain the single-phase microstructure and within the compositional window of the FeMnNiGeSi system. The effect may not hold if the annealing temperature is high enough to induce unwanted phase changes or extensive grain growth.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative trade-off between reduced hysteresis and any possible slight reduction in peak entropy change remains uncertain and must be characterized experimentally. Additionally, the sensitivity of the magnetocaloric response to variations in annealing time and temperature needs further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA samples: one set as-deposited and another subjected to a controlled low-temperature annealing protocol. Under identical low-field magnetic-cooling cycle conditions, measure isothermal magnetization curves, perform AC susceptibility tests, and determine the magnetic entropy change (ΔS) through calorimetric or magnetic methods.
measurements: Magnetization vs. applied field hysteresis loops at various temperatures around the transition
Differential scanning calorimetry (or equivalent) under applied magnetic field to quantify ΔS(T)
AC susceptibility measurements to assess frequency-dependent behavior related to domain dynamics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis (e.g., loop narrowing, lower coercivity) without a concomitant large drop (>20%) in the measured magnetic entropy change relative to the as-deposited samples, then the hypothesis that local chemical inhomogeneities are the dominant mechanism governing both the magnetocaloric effect and hysteresis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Relative cooling powers (RCP) for equivalent bulk and nano-sized compounds are comparable in value: 166 J/kg vs. 175 J/kg (4 T) for bulk and nano-sized with x = 0.02 This is due to the wide effective temperature range of entropy change δTFWHM in nanocrystalline samples. All values of RCP are high and comparable with relevant compounds reported in the literature. Bulk samples with x = 0.3 exhibits positive entropy change at antiferromagnetic-ferromagnetic transition temperature Magnetic entropy changes and magnetic parameters of the bulk polycrystalline samples indicate them as potential candidates for magnetocaloric materials. Possibly, they can be combined in construction of multistep refrigeration processes to increase their temperature range and effectiveness. The nanocrystalline samples, which show comparatively lower maximum entropy change are moved to the immediate background of the picture of usable magnetocaloric compounds but could, possibly, be still useful in future developments.

Changes in −ΔSmax as well as the changes in the shape of the −ΔS(ΔH, T) curves are important to MCE when applied to magnetic refrigeration, as they may lead to changes in the overall refrigerant capacity (RC). RC in general is the figure of merit used to compare MCE materials giving the total heat transfer of the material over a typical refrigeration cycle. RC for a given ΔH is calculated as the integral of −ΔS(T) over a temperature range of interest: Here, TR1 and TR2 are traditionally taken to be the temperatures corresponding to the FWHM of the −ΔS(T) feature on the low and high temperature sides of the peak, respectively. We do not consider hysteretic losses here, as the M(H) loops showed negligible hysteresis, though that can be important in many systems. Figure 5 shows RC as a function of ΔH for both the annealed and as-rolled samples. The RC of 36 J/kg for a 1 T field change puts these HEAs below many other materials designed to operate in the 100–200 K range, though several factors related to pragmatic engineering issues (e.g., ductility, corrosion resistance, high thermal conductivity) may make up for this.
